channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Even substitute PFAS cause metabolic stress in zebrafish embryos
item.description: Publishing in the Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances, researchers from Kyushu University used zebrafish embryos to study the health effects of the PFAS called PFBS (perfluorobutanesulfonic acid), a substitute PFAS thought to be safer than traditional compounds. They found that while PFBS did not generate any obvious external dysfunction, the compound still gets absorbed and accumulates in the zebrafish embryo. Results showed that PFBS caused disruptions in the metabolic pathways for sugars and fat, which led to oxidative stress. Embryos also showed physical impairments in heart function, facial development, nervous system development and visual response.

item.title: Office lighting experiments raise questions about human health
item.description: If you spend your workday under fluorescent lights, new research from Michigan State University suggests your body may notice. In a study of animals that, like people, are active during the day, researchers found that living under fluorescent office lighting was linked to weaker daily rhythms, higher rates of diabetic-range blood glucose and less active sperm compared with living under daylight-equivalent light. But a single hour of midday light helped make up the difference.

item.title: Study finds gradebook data can help predict risk of drug use in adolescents
item.description: GPA has long been a benchmark for measuring success in students. It can also do more than indicate academic accomplishment: Health studies have established a strong correlation between GPA and the risk of unhealthy behaviors in adolescents, including substance abuse.

item.title: Parkinson's-linked protein may sabotage the brain's waste disposal system
item.description: A protein's shape can make all the difference between keeping the body running smoothly and contributing to disease. A protein called α-synuclein (α-syn), under normal conditions, helps neurons release neurotransmitters by interacting with tiny structures called synaptic vesicles at the ends of nerve cells. The accumulation of misfolded versions of the same protein can lead to Parkinson's disease, a nervous system disorder that affects movement and gets worse over time. The clumped-up protein also collects in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) surrounding the brain and in the brain's outer border tissue, known as the dura mater.

item.title: Lifetime trauma linked to dementia and memory problems in older Australians, study
item.description: The study of more than 1,800 older Australians found that people who had experienced lifetime trauma were more likely to have mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia and performed worse on working memory and executive function tests.

item.title: The history and future of neuroeconomics: Q&A
item.description: So, what exactly is neuroeconomics? The Society for Neuroeconomics website describes it as a field that "represents the confluence of economics, psychology, and neuroscience in the study of human decision making." But for Antonio Rangel (BS '93), Caltech's Bing professor of neuroscience, behavioral biology and economics and past president of the Society for Neuroeconomics, the aim of the field is much more profound.

item.title: A gut microbe shields mice from Parkinson's-like brain damage
item.description: Parkinson's disease is usually thought of as a brain disease, but many patients notice gut trouble—constipation above all—years or even decades before their hands begin to tremble. That timing has led researchers to ask whether the illness sometimes begins in the intestine, and whether treating the gut early could change what later happens in the brain.

item.title: Common skin cancer rising faster in women
item.description: New research led by QIMR Berghofer has uncovered a decades-long increase in the rates of a common form of skin cancer across Australia and Europe, highlighting a growing but underrecognized public health challenge.

item.title: Canine companionship, with a catch: Health effects of big-city dog ownership differ by location
item.description: How neighborhoods support healthy aging is a key question for aging societies. Yet little is known about how dog walking, an everyday activity, interacts with the neighborhood environment in dense Asian cities.

item.title: Stress more strongly linked to poorer quality of life among adults with multiple chronic conditions
item.description: Perceived stress is more strongly associated with poorer health-related quality of life among adults living with two or more chronic conditions than among those without chronic conditions, according to a new study from the University of Eastern Finland.

item.title: America's long-term care system needs help: Can Europe provide a model for how to improve it?
item.description: For millions of Americans, long-term care presents enormous financial, logistical and emotional challenges. Private long-term care insurance is prohibitively expensive or simply unavailable, and most older Americans aren't eligible for Medicaid until they exhaust nearly all their financial resources.

item.title: Effective obesity treatments reach few eligible teens, study finds
item.description: Despite the arrival of powerful new anti-obesity medications and growing evidence supporting weight-loss surgery for adolescents, the vast majority of eligible teens are receiving neither treatment, according to a new study from Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago published in JAMA Pediatrics.

item.title: Children who travel further for common surgery have more complications and longer hospital stays
item.description: Nearly one in eight children undergoing a common inpatient surgical procedure lived more than 60 miles (97 kilometers) from the hospital where they received care. These children had higher odds of complications, longer hospital stays and higher hospital charges than children who lived closer, according to a study published in the Journal of the American College of Surgeons (JACS).

item.title: Bioengineers create portable tool to spot preterm birth risk
item.description: Biomedical engineers at Florida International University have built a portable imaging device designed to detect early signs of preterm labor risk in about five seconds. The system, called PPRIM (Portable Preterm Imaging), could flag risk up to three months earlier than current screening methods.

item.title: Study identifies potential strategy to reduce breast reconstruction complications after proton therapy
item.description: Radiation therapy is sometimes needed after mastectomy and breast reconstruction for breast cancer. However, patients with implant-based reconstruction who receive radiation therapy have a higher risk of capsular contracture, a complication in which scar tissue tightens around the implant. In more severe cases, it can cause breast pain, firmness or distortion and may require additional surgery.

item.title: Five-year survival from pediatric cancer rises to nearly 90% overall, but disparities by race and cancer type remain
item.description: Nearly nine in 10 young people with cancer were alive five years after diagnosis by 2017—up from six in 10 in 1975, according to the first comprehensive update of U.S. childhood cancer survival statistics in over a decade published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute.

item.title: Experiences reshape brain cell connections, synapse mapping reveals
item.description: Experiences and changes in the environment cause widespread alterations in connections between brain cells, influencing brain activity, research suggests. Using a novel technology to map and study billions of individual brain cell connections, scientists have found that mice exposed to an enriched environment showed changes in different populations of synapses—the connections through which nerve cells communicate—across many brain regions.

item.title: Fewer than 5% of US military veterans may achieve optimal heart health
item.description: Fewer than 5% of U.S. military veterans may achieve optimal cardiovascular health based on the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 metrics, highlighting an urgent opportunity to improve prevention and help veterans live longer, healthier lives, according to a new scientific statement published in Circulation.

item.title: Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak
item.description: Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease.

item.title: Study reveals gaps in women's heart health care in New Zealand
item.description: A review of 25 years of New Zealand research has revealed significant gaps in women's heart health care, highlighting opportunities to improve diagnosis, treatment and outcomes. Published in the New Zealand Medical Journal, the systematic review, co-led by Dr. Kylie Short of Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC), identified a significant gender data gap, with just 26% of studies specifically focused on differences between women and men.

item.title: School bullying tied to symptoms and diagnosis of PTSD
item.description: School bullying has been linked to lower academic achievement and increased mental health problems, making it a critical concern for the field of educational psychology. Understanding the psychological consequences of bullying is essential for educators, school psychologists and policymakers to develop effective interventions that support students' well-being and learning outcomes. One ongoing debate is whether bullying qualifies as a traumatic event that may lead to posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and diagnosis.

item.title: 1 in 3 births are induced. It can be lifesaving, but it's also linked to more complications
item.description: Around one in three women in Australia now have their labors induced rather than having them start naturally, or spontaneously.

item.title: How conversations shape decisions about dementia care
item.description: When someone is living with dementia, decisions about their care can have a significant impact on their health and quality of life. But how are these decisions made, particularly when family members or friends are also involved?

item.title: Cannabis addiction in pregnancy linked to higher risk of postpartum psychiatric crises
item.description: Women diagnosed with cannabis use disorder during pregnancy were more likely to end up in an emergency room for a psychiatric problem in the year after giving birth, according to a study of more than 2 million California deliveries.

item.title: Going to the park at least once a week can improve children's mental health
item.description: Children who visit parks and playgrounds at least once a week may have better mental health and social development as they grow up. That's according to a new study by the University of Exeter, published in Epidemiology and Community Health. The paper is titled "Park Visits and Social-Emotional Development throughout Childhood: A Longitudinal Analysis of ALSPAC."

item.title: Successful sleep apnea treatment may lead to unexpected weight gain
item.description: A new study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) and Soroka University Medical Center may have uncovered a biological mechanism behind why many adults and children gain weight following successful treatment for obstructive sleep apnea. The research, conducted on mice and published in Scientific Reports, suggests that the body retains a persistent "metabolic memory" that continues to drive increased appetite even after normal breathing is restored.

item.title: Study identifies antidepressants that get patients well and keep them well
item.description: Worldwide, nearly 6% of people experience depression. Many of them continue taking antidepressants after achieving symptomatic improvement, among other reasons to prevent a relapse of depression. An international team of researchers investigated which antidepressants, if any, can not only get patients well but also keep them well (sustained response).

item.title: UK regulatory systems for food and drink identify only around half of processed/ultraprocessed products as unhealthy
item.description: Current U.K. regulatory systems for food and drink identify only around half of processed and ultraprocessed products as unhealthy—in other words, those that contain excess fat, salt, sugar and energy density—finds research published in BMJ Medicine. But new nutrient profiling, based on official U.K. dietary guidance, classifies more than 90% of these products as unhealthy. A single unified regulatory system, using agreed definitions, that is aligned with this guidance may offer the best way forward, say the researchers.

item.title: Deaf patients get a raw deal in NHS hospitals, illustrative case history suggests
item.description: Deaf patients get a raw deal in NHS hospitals, suggests an illustrative case history of a deaf person's experience as an inpatient, published in the online journal BMJ Case Reports. During his hospital stay, reasonable adjustments to facilitate access to services—a key tenet of U.K. disability legislation—weren't made; the need for a professional British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter wasn't recognized soon enough; and frontline staff weren't adequately trained in how to support him.

item.title: Government guidance indicates 95% of processed foods are unhealthy
item.description: More than 95% of processed or ultra-processed food products would be classified as unhealthy under UK government dietary guidance, according to new UCL-led research. The study, published in BMJ Medicine, found that the official public health definitions used to identify and regulate food and drink products in the U.K. varied widely in what proportion of processed and ultraprocessed products they classed as unhealthy, while systems such as traffic light labels failed to identify more than half of these unhealthy packaged foods.
